spans.note: Repeated page header and blank lines before the title

spans.assertion: the analyzed sample consisted of 2,053 male first-division soccer players (Spain, Germany, England, France) and 3,147 referees they encountered

spans.note: States the two research questions being tested

spans.assertion: fit a Poisson multi-level model (offset by number of games) to test whether red card counts were predicted by skintone, and whether that relationship was moderated by prejudice measures
controlled for player position and included referee and player as random effects in the model
found referees were 41% more likely to award red cards to dark- versus light-skin-toned players
found this skintone effect was not influenced by implicit or explicit prejudice measures
the analysis supports the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to darker- versus lighter-skinned players
this effect was not influenced by implicit or explicit measures of racial bias from the referee's home country

spans.note: Repeated page header and blank lines

spans.assertion: the dependent variable for all analyses was the number of red cards given within a player-referee dyad
decided a Poisson distribution was the best fit for the data given its count nature
used the log number of games per dyad as the offset variable to account for the number of interactions a dyad had
checked whether the Poisson equidispersion assumption (mean equal to variance) held for the data
found the mean (M = 0.0125) and variance (σ2 = 0.0127) were approximately equal, so overdispersion was not an issue
noted many zero counts in the dataset, reflecting the rarity of red cards in a game

spans.note: Cites Nussbaum, Elsadat, & Khago (2008) on Poisson being suited to rare events over large numbers of observations

spans.assertion: saw no indication the large number of zero events came from anything other than the rarity of red cards, and did not treat the zeros as generated by a different (zero-inflated Poisson) process
checked the inter-rater reliability between the two skintone raters
found inter-rater reliability was high, r = .92
averaged the two raters' ratings to create a single skintone variable
no complete cases were excluded from any analysis
missing variables were excluded pair-wise
all analyses were conducted using R 3.0.2 on OSX 10.9.3
used an alpha of .05 for all tests
dichotomized the skintone rating into "light skin" (average rating < 3) and "dark skin" (average rating > 3) because of concern about treating the ordinal Likert scale as continuous/interval
deliberately left out players rated "neutral" by both raters from the light/dark dichotomy

spans.note: Rationale that the dichotomy captures relevant differences without assuming linearity of the rating measure

spans.assertion: ran a GLM with a Poisson link testing whether the number of red cards (offset by log games) differed by skintone
included position in the model because some positions (e.g., goalkeeper) were felt to be inherently less likely to receive red cards
found dark skin toned players were 12.3% more likely to get a red card than light skin players, but this was not significantly different from zero: exp(β) = 1.123, z(107774) = -1.6, p = .11
concluded from this test that soccer referees were not more likely to give red cards to dark skin toned players compared to light skin toned players

spans.note: Repeated page header and blank lines

spans.assertion: aggregated the data by referee country and player skin color, creating a new dataset with games-played and red-card variables for dark and light skin toned players per referee country
initially tried creating a "relative risk" ratio variable comparing the probability of a red card for dark versus light skin toned players
abandoned the relative-risk ratio approach because many probabilities were zero, leaving too few data points, and instead decided to model red card counts as a Poisson distribution as in Hypothesis 1
included position in the model
used the number of red cards given to dark skin toned players (offset by log games with dark skin toned players) as the dependent variable
included the probability of giving a light skin toned player a red card as a covariate, to account for a referee's general propensity to give red cards
included position as before, and included implicit (mean IAT) and explicit (mean Exp) prejudice scores as predictors separately in each model
found neither the IAT nor Exp prejudice measure significantly predicted increased red cards to dark skin toned players (IAT: exp(β)=1.68, z(123)=0.24, p=.81; Exp: exp(β)=1.04, z(123)=0.11, p=.92)

spans.note: States that the approach changed after receiving feedback from other groups

spans.assertion: realized they had neglected to account for repeated instances of referees and players in the dataset, leaving non-independence in the data
decided to address the non-independence critique by including referee and player as random effects in the final models
changed the Hypothesis 2 approach to accommodate the added random-effects level
decided to use the skintone measure as a continuous variable instead of dichotomizing it

spans.note: Notes reviewers questioned the dichotomization and that linearity concerns are still believed valid

spans.assertion: based the decision to use continuous skintone on literature (e.g., Lovell, 2000) suggesting a dichotomized skintone representation is inappropriate for non-US cultures such as Brazil and may not suit everyone in this sample

spans.note: Blank line and Hypothesis 1 restated (final approach)

spans.assertion: ran a Poisson-distributed GLM using number of red cards as the dependent variable with log(games) as the offset
included position as a covariate and referee and player as random effects
used the continuous measure of skin tone as the predictor of interest
found skin tone significantly predicted red cards, with probability increasing 41% for dark versus light skin tone: exp(β) = 1.41 [95% CI 1.13–1.75], z = 3.08, p = .002

spans.note: Repeated page header and blank lines
Blank line and Hypothesis 2 restated (final approach)

spans.assertion: ran two additional models with implicit (mean IAT) and explicit (mean Exp) measures included separately to test whether the Hypothesis 1 effect was stronger for referees from high-prejudice countries
modeled the interaction between IAT or Exp and skintone as the predictor of interest to capture whether the skintone-red card relationship changed with referee country-level prejudice
found neither interaction was significant: IAT exp(β) = 0.13 [95% CI .0002–68.06], z = -0.65, p = .52; Exp exp(β) = 1.09 [95% CI 0.42–2.84], z = 0.18, p = .86
these null interactions suggest the general skintone bias in red card distribution was not influenced by whether the referee was from a country high in skintone prejudice
the analysis confirms the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark skin toned players than light skin toned players
found no evidence this effect was related to whether a referee came from a country with high or low skintone prejudice, based on implicit and explicit measures

spans.note: Restates the earlier decision to use skintone continuously rather than as a light/dark binary
Expresses ongoing concern about the quality and linearity of the skintone ratings and unknown provenance, which could affect validity of conclusions

spans.assertion: judged the data well suited to test the first research question, despite rating flaws, citing supporting literature that skintone as a range is a strong predictor of bias

judged the results limited in generalizability because the sample, drawn from top-tier European leagues, has a high prevalence of European referees not representative of the broader population of soccer referees
judged that dyads involving non-European referees likely arise from exceptional/unusual situations, which could systematically bias both player behavior and referee red-card decisions
judged the dataset far less well suited to test the second research question

spans.note: Notes the implicit/explicit bias measures were potentially promising but their quality and representativeness are unknown and expected to vary by country
Notes that even if the measures accurately represented a country's attitude, it is unknown how much a given referee identifies with that country or shares the popular opinion
States these factors make it very difficult to draw meaningful conclusions about the second hypothesis

spans.assertion: expects a different, harder-to-obtain dataset would have been needed to answer the second research question with reasonable certainty
